## Find the gatekeeper: who can stop or see it {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

**The case:** an agent hands you a Tron address, a T-address, that received USDT from a fraud victim. The agent asks two things: can anyone still stop the money, and how far can you follow it?

**This morning** you read where a trace stops at an exchange (04-FO) and which rules make the business keep records (05-FO). Day 3 (05-EF) showed that Tether can freeze USDT on Ethereum. This lesson finds the gatekeepers that sit on the ledger itself, in four parts:

1. **Tron reads like Ethereum:** what carries over, and what Energy changes.
2. **USDT on Tron:** read a transfer, a sweep and a freeze; the issuer is the gatekeeper.
3. **Permissioned ledgers:** the operator is the gatekeeper, and the trace stops at its edge.
4. **CBDCs and the Fabric demo:** a central bank as operator, then a live network.

**By the end:** for any ledger in a case, name the gatekeeper, say what it can do (stop a payment, see the records, or both), and say what you can still read from outside.

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide opens the lesson with a case and one question to ask of every ledger: who is the gatekeeper? It matters here because the morning's two lessons put the gatekeepers off the chain, at exchanges and in the rules; this lesson finds the ones written into the ledger. Emphasize the objective: the practice and the review come back to it.

**Key Points**
- Students already know three things this lesson builds on. Day 3 (05-EF, Tokens and Stablecoins) showed that USDT's contract lets Tether freeze an address on Ethereum. This morning's 04-FO showed that a trace into an exchange stops at the deposit address, because the exchange's own books say who owns what after the sweep. 05-FO showed which rules make that exchange keep records.
- The case runs through parts 1 and 2: a T-address that received a victim's USDT. Part 1 shows how to read the address at all; part 2 asks whether the issuer can still stop the money. Parts 3 and 4 bring the second case: funds that leave Tron for a ledger only its operator can read.
- "Gatekeeper" is the lesson's one word for whoever can stop a payment or decide who sees it. On Tron, for USDT, that is Tether. On a permissioned ledger, it is the operator.
- The afternoon lab reads a Tron snapshot with the same three reads part 2 works: a transfer, a sweep, a freeze.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the case and leave both of the agent's questions open; the lesson answers them.
2. Read the link back: 04-FO, 05-FO, then day 3's freeze. Name the four parts.
3. Read the objective aloud. Each of the first three parts ends with a check every student answers, and the close asks the objective again.
4. Time plan, 50 minutes: opening 2, part 1 (Tron) 9, part 2 (USDT on Tron) 15, part 3 (permissioned ledgers) 10, part 4 (CBDCs and the demo set-up) 6, close (practice, answers, review, next) 8.

**Sources**
- @tether_usdttroncontract_2026
- @hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_privatedata_2022

:::

## What carries over: T-addresses and 19 of 27 {.smaller}

[]{#tron-works-like-ethereum-with-t-addresses}[]{#elected-producers-final-after-19-confirm}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

- **Same key, same 20 bytes:** a Tron address is made as an Ethereum one is, from a secp256k1 key and Keccak-256. Tron adds the prefix `0x41` and encodes the 21 bytes in Base58Check: 34 characters, starting with **T** [@tron_accounts_2026].
- **Same token standard:** TRC-20 is "fully compatible with Ethereum's ERC-20 at the interface level" [@tron_trc20_2026], so a USDT transfer emits a `Transfer` log, as on day 3.
- **New: 27 producers, final after 19.** "Twenty-seven Super Representatives (SRs), elected by stakers' votes," make a block about every 3 seconds. A block is **solidified** (final) once at least 19 distinct SRs have each produced a block at or above it [@tron_consensus_2026].
- For the analyst: read Tron as you read Ethereum, from solidified data only [@tron_api_2026].

:::

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

::: {style="font-size: .8em;"}

Tron's own example [@tron_accounts_2026]:

| Form | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Tron, hex | `412a260a110bc7b03f19c40a0bd04ff2c5dcb57594` |
| Tron, Base58Check | `TDp4x8kCJ6aHz8wnqZgkaVQAm2ajH1og3L` |
| Ethereum form | `0x2a260a110bc7b03f19c40a0bd04ff2c5dcb57594` |

Drop the `41` and the same 20 bytes are an Ethereum address. The same 20 bytes on both chains mean the same key, so one controller: a **lead** to confirm, not a finding.

:::

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide shows what an analyst who can read Ethereum already knows about Tron, and the one new thing about its blocks. It matters here because the case is a T-address: students must be able to read it, and to tie it to an Ethereum address if the same key controls both. Emphasize the table: one key, two address forms.

**Key Points**
- A Tron address is derived the way day 1's 04-CP derived an Ethereum one: the public key from secp256k1, then the last 20 bytes of its Keccak-256 hash. Tron puts the byte `0x41` in front, which makes 21 bytes, then encodes them in Base58Check, which gives 34 characters starting with T.
- So the table's hex form is the Ethereum address with `41` in front. Strip the `41` and you have the Ethereum form. Because both forms come from one key, an address that appears in both forms on the two chains points to one controller. It stays a lead, because the analyst still has to confirm it with activity or a source.
- TRC-20 tokens have ERC-20's functions and events, so a USDT transfer on Tron logs `Transfer` as on Ethereum. Day 3's reading carries over unchanged.
- What is new is the block producers. 27 elected Super Representatives make blocks under delegated proof of stake, about every 3 seconds, and a block is solidified once 19 distinct SRs have built at or above it. Day 1 (01-CM) taught "solidified"; here it means the analyst reads only blocks that can no longer change, and java-tron serves those on its own endpoints.
- The producers are not the gatekeeper for USDT. They make blocks; the issuer freezes, as part 2 shows.

**Walkthrough**
1. Point at the hex row, cover the `41` with a finger, and read the Ethereum row beneath it.
2. Ask: the same 20 bytes appear on Ethereum and on Tron in one case. What can you say? (Expected answer: probably one controller, because one key makes both; a lead to confirm, not a finding.)
3. Ask a student what "solidified" means before you read that bullet. (Expected answer: at least 19 of the 27 SRs have built on it, so it no longer rolls back.)

**Sources**
- @tron_accounts_2026
- @tron_trc20_2026
- @tron_consensus_2026
- @tron_api_2026

:::

## Energy pays for a USDT move: who staked it? {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="56%"}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

- **Wrong idea:** the sender pays the fee, as on Ethereum. **Not always** on Tron: the fee is paid in resources that another account can supply.
- **Right:** a USDT transfer is a contract call, so it uses **Energy** (computation); its bytes use **Bandwidth** [@tron_resourcemodel_2026].
- Energy has no free quota. An account must "stake (or receive delegated) TRX to obtain it, or rely on the TRX-burn fallback" [@tron_resourcemodel_2026]. So one of three paid:
  1. the sender, by **staking** TRX;
  2. another account, by **delegating** Energy;
  3. the sender, by **burning** TRX, which another account may have sent it.
- For the analyst: an address with **no TRX of its own** can still move USDT. Note who paid, not only who sent.

:::

:::

::: {.column width="44%"}

```{dot}
digraph Energy {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];
  edge [color="#64748b", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9];
  S [label="Sender stakes TRX", fillcolor="#fef3c7"];
  D [label="Another account\ndelegates Energy", fillcolor="#fee2e2"];
  B [label="Sender burns TRX", fillcolor="#e5e7eb"];
  A [label="USDT transfer", fillcolor="#dbeafe"];
  S -> A [label="1"];
  D -> A [label="2"];
  B -> A [label="3"];
}
```

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide explains Tron's fee model in the one way an analyst needs: who paid for a USDT transfer. It matters here because on Tron the sender and the payer can be different accounts, so the payer is a second link the analyst can follow. Emphasize the wrong idea first: students from Ethereum assume the sender pays.

**Key Points**
- On Ethereum the sender pays gas in ETH. Students carry that over, and on Tron it is wrong, because Tron charges in two resources instead of a coin.
- Bandwidth covers the bytes a transaction stores; Energy covers the computation of a contract call. A USDT transfer calls the USDT contract, so it needs Energy.
- Energy has no free quota, so it must come from somewhere: TRX the sender staked, Energy another account delegated to the sender, or TRX the sender burns at the moment of the transfer.
- The second and third routes let an address that holds only USDT move it: another account delegates Energy, or sends a little TRX for the sender to burn. Either way, a second account paid, and that payment is on chain.
- This is the payer the lab asks about this afternoon, so the analyst asks of every sweep: who staked it?

**Walkthrough**
1. Ask first: on Ethereum, who pays the fee? (The sender, in ETH.) Then read the wrong idea and why it is wrong here.
2. Walk the three arrows of the diagram: stake, delegate, burn.
3. Ask: an address holds 5,000 USDT and no TRX, and it sends the USDT. Who paid? (Expected answer: someone else, either by delegating Energy or by sending TRX that was burned; find that account.)

**Sources**
- @tron_resourcemodel_2026

:::

## Half of all USDT sits on Tron {.smaller}

- Of 180.1 billion USDT in circulation, **92.4 billion (51%)** is on Tron and **70.9 billion (39%)** on Ethereum [@defillama_tetherbychain_2026] [31 Oct 2026]{.asof}.
- Day 3 showed that stablecoins carry most illicit volume [@chainalysis_2026cryptocrimereport_2026] [Jan 2026]{.asof}. Tron holds over half of the leading stablecoin's supply, so a USDT case will often run through Tron.
- For the analyst: the Day 9 trace and the Day 10 scenario both include Tron USDT.

::: {.callout-note}
Supply by chain moves daily; read the current figure, with its date, before you quote it.
:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide explains why a US analyst needs Tron at all: it holds more USDT than any other chain. It matters here because students who know only Ethereum will meet Tron in most stablecoin cases. Emphasize the date: these figures change daily.

**Key Points**
- About half of circulating USDT is on Tron and about two-fifths on Ethereum, as DefiLlama read them on 31 Oct 2026.
- Day 3 (05-EF) gave the Chainalysis finding that stablecoins carry most illicit volume [Jan 2026]{.asof}. Put the two together and Tron is where an analyst most often meets illicit USDT.
- The day 9 trace and the day 10 scenario both include Tron USDT, so the reading in part 2 returns.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the figures with their date.
2. Ask why the date matters. (Expected answer: supply moves between chains daily, so an undated share may be wrong.)

**Sources**
- @defillama_tetherbychain_2026
- @chainalysis_2026cryptocrimereport_2026

:::

## Check: T-address, 0x address: which chain? {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

The agent's case file holds two USDT addresses:

- `TDp4x8kCJ6aHz8wnqZgkaVQAm2ajH1og3L`
- `0x2a260a110bc7b03f19c40a0bd04ff2c5dcb57594`

**Write one line:** which chain do you read for each, and what does the pair suggest?

::: {.fragment}
**Answer:** the T-address is Tron; the 0x address is an EVM chain, most often Ethereum, so check which. These two carry the same 20 bytes, so one key made both: a lead that one person controls both, to confirm before you write it [@tron_accounts_2026].

**Part 1 in one line:** Tron reads like Ethereum, with a T in front of the same 20 bytes; what is new is who pays the Energy [@tron_accounts_2026; @tron_resourcemodel_2026].
:::

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide closes part 1 with a check every student answers: tell the chain from the address, and read what a shared 20 bytes means. It matters here because a case file often mixes Tron and Ethereum addresses, and reading the wrong chain finds nothing. Emphasize that the pair is a lead, not a finding.

**Key Points**
- Expected answer: the T-address is Tron. The 0x address is an EVM chain, most often Ethereum, but other EVM chains use the same format, so check which.
- The pair is Tron's own example from the address slide: strip the `41` from the hex form and the bytes match. One key made both, so one controller is likely; the analyst confirms it with activity or a source before writing it.
- The part 1 synthesis, on the slide, carries the one new idea, Energy, into part 2.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the two addresses aloud.
2. Give every student thirty seconds to write one line.
3. Take two or three answers, then reveal the answer and the part 1 line.

**Sources**
- @tron_accounts_2026
- @tron_resourcemodel_2026

:::

## Worked: a USDT transfer on Tron, field by field {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

The case's first read: the victim's payment into the T-address. The addresses and amounts are made up; USDT's contract and its 6 decimals are real [@tether_usdttroncontract_2026].

| Field | What the record shows | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contract called | `TR7NHqjeKQxGTCi8q8ZY4pL8otSzgjLj6t` | The real USDT contract, not a copy (day 3's check) |
| `Transfer` log: from | `TVictim…` (made up) | The sender, who signed the call |
| `Transfer` log: to | `TCase…` (made up) | The case's address, the payee |
| `Transfer` log: value | `2500000000` | Divide by 10^6^: **2,500 USDT** |
| Block and time | block N, solidified | Final: 19 SRs have built on it |
| Receipt: Energy | used Energy, none staked; TRX burned | The sender paid, by burning (payer 3) |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

**Say it:** "On [date], `TVictim…` sent 2,500 USDT to `TCase…` in solidified block N, and paid for it by burning TRX."

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide works the first of the lab's three reads on the case's own payment: a USDT transfer on Tron, one field at a time. It matters here because the afternoon lab asks students to do exactly this read on real data, and this is the first time they see it done on Tron. Emphasize that every line on day 3's Ethereum read appears again; only the receipt's Energy line is new.

**Key Points**
- The first field is the contract: day 3 taught that a token's address, not its name, says which token it is, so the analyst checks it is USDT's real contract.
- The `Transfer` log names the sender and receiver and carries the raw value. USDT's contract on Tron reports 6 decimals, as on Ethereum, so 2,500,000,000 is 2,500 USDT.
- The block must be solidified, from part 1, so the read cannot change.
- The receipt's Energy line is the new field: here the sender had none staked and none delegated, so it burned TRX. In a sweep, the next slide, a different account pays, and that is the link to look for.
- The sentence states chain facts only, so it takes no confidence word. The values are made up so that the lab's own read stays fresh.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read each row left to right: field, value, meaning.
2. At the value row, ask a student to do the division before you show it.
3. At the Energy row, ask which of the three payers this is. (Payer 3: the sender burned TRX.)
4. Read the sentence aloud and point out that it carries no confidence word: every part is read off the chain.

**Sources**
- @tether_usdttroncontract_2026
- @tron_trc20_2026
- @tron_consensus_2026
- @tron_resourcemodel_2026

:::

## Worked: a deposit, its sweep, who paid Energy {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

The case's second read: where the 2,500 USDT went. Values made up.

| Time | What the chain shows |
| --- | --- |
| 10:00 | `TCase…` receives 2,500 USDT (the last slide) |
| 10:20 | Account `TPayer…` sends `TCase…` 15 TRX; `TCase…` has no other TRX |
| 10:32 | `TCase…` sends its **whole** USDT balance to `THot…`, burning the 15 TRX for the Energy |
| | `THot…` appears in an exchange's own published list of its wallets |

**Read it:**

1. **Whole balance, one destination, soon after:** a sweep, the deposit-address pattern from 04-FO.
2. **Who paid:** not `TCase…`. `TPayer…` sent the TRX that was burned (payer 3, funded by someone else).
3. **Label:** the exchange publishes `THot…` as its own.
4. **Say it:** "Moderate confidence that `TCase…` is a deposit address at the exchange: it swept its whole balance to a wallet the exchange publishes, and a third account paid for the sweep. Name the deposit, not the sweep."

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide works the lab's second read: a deposit, its sweep, and who paid for the sweep. It matters here because the case's T-address turns out to be an exchange deposit address, which tells the agent where the money went and who holds the records. Emphasize step 2: on Tron, the payer is evidence of its own.

**Key Points**
- 04-FO taught the sweep: a deposit address sends on what it received, whole for tokens, to the exchange's main wallet. The same pattern appears here.
- New on Tron: the deposit address holds no TRX, so someone else must pay. Here `TPayer…` sends 15 TRX shortly before the sweep, and the sweep burns it. Another account could delegate Energy instead, payer 2.
- The exchange's own published wallet list labels `THot…`, so two lines agree: the sweep's shape and the label.
- Moderate, not High: both lines come from the same sweep, and no source names `TCase…` itself. As 04-FO taught, the analyst names the deposit, because the exchange, not the chain, knows the account holder.
- The values are made up so that the lab's own read stays fresh.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the timeline top to bottom.
2. Before the steps, ask: what is `TCase…`? Take one or two answers.
3. Work the four steps aloud. At step 2, ask which of the three payers this is.
4. Ask: what would lower the confidence? (Expected answer: no published label on `THot…`, so only the shape remains.)

**Sources**
- @tron_resourcemodel_2026
- @victor_clustering_2020

:::

## USDT on Tron: same freeze, same owner rule {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}

- **Same as day 3:** Tron's USDT is the same `TetherToken` design, with the owner-only `addBlackList`, `removeBlackList` and `destroyBlackFunds`, and the `AddedBlackList` event [@tether_usdttroncontract_2026; @tether_tethertokensource_2017].
- **Different on Tron:** the owner is a multisignature wallet contract, `TBPxhVAsuzoFnKyXtc1o2UySEydPHgATto`, with three keys, two of which must agree [@tether_usdttroncontract_2026; @tether_usdtmultisig_2026] [5 Nov 2026]{.asof}. An owner can change, so read it at the time.
- For the analyst: Tether is the gatekeeper for USDT on Tron. The SRs make the blocks, but only the owner can freeze.

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{dot}
digraph Freeze {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11];
  edge [color="#64748b", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9];
  O [label="Owner\n(2-of-3 multisig wallet)", fillcolor="#fee2e2"];
  C [label="USDT contract\nTR7NH…Lj6t", fillcolor="#dbeafe"];
  L [label="AddedBlackList\nevent", fillcolor="#fef3c7"];
  O -> C [label="addBlackList(addr)"];
  C -> L [label="logs"];
}
```

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide carries day 3's freeze onto Tron and names the one difference. It matters here because the agent's first question was whether anyone can still stop the money, and on Tron the answer is the same issuer with the same controls. Emphasize that the issuer, not the network, is the gatekeeper for the token.

**Key Points**
- Day 3 taught the three owner-only functions and the event on Ethereum. Tron's USDT contract has the same ones, so nothing about the freeze needs relearning.
- What differs is the owner: on Tron it is a multisignature wallet with three keys, of which two must sign. That is read from the chain, and an owner can change, hence the date.
- A freeze shows up as an `AddedBlackList` event from the USDT contract; that event is what the lab looks for.

**Walkthrough**
1. Ask a student to recall day 3: what can a frozen address still do? (It can still receive; it cannot send.)
2. Point at the diagram: owner, contract, event.

**Sources**
- @tether_usdttroncontract_2026
- @tether_usdtmultisig_2026
- @tether_tethertokensource_2017

:::

## A freeze is true only at the time of the read {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

- **Two questions, two answers** [@tether_usdttroncontract_2026]:
  - *Is it frozen?* `isBlackListed(address)` answers for the block you read it at.
  - *When was it frozen?* The `AddedBlackList` event gives the block and time.
- A later `RemovedBlackList` undoes a freeze, so a status read today may not be the status then [@tether_tethertokensource_2017].

**Worked: the snapshot's freeze.** On 23 April 2026, Tether said it had frozen \$344 million in USDT across two addresses, with the U.S. Government [@tether_freeze344m_2026]. The lab reads both from the chain:

| Read | Gives |
| --- | --- |
| The `AddedBlackList` events | The block and time each address was added, and which of the owner wallet's keys sent it (from the transaction) |
| `isBlackListed` at the snapshot's block | Whether each is still frozen **at that block** |

**Say it:** "USDT's contract blacklisted the two addresses in block N on 23 April 2026; at block M, read on date D, they remain blacklisted." Who owns them, and why, comes from sources, not the chain.

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide teaches the analyst's habit for freeze status, date it, and works it on the freeze the lab reads. It matters here because a status read today may differ from the status on the day of the transfers, and both may differ next week. Emphasize the difference between state (now) and events (when).

**Key Points**
- `isBlackListed` gives the status at the block it is read at; the `AddedBlackList` and `RemovedBlackList` events give the history.
- Day 3 covered what a freeze leaves on chain. What is new here is that a removal can undo it, so a status without a block and date can mislead.
- The worked case is the public one: Tether's 23 April 2026 statement that it froze \$344 million across two addresses with the U.S. Government. The lab reads the events and the status from its snapshot.
- The sentence has two parts: chain facts, with their blocks, and what only sources say. The lab fills in N, M and D from the snapshot; leave them as letters here so the lab's answers stay fresh.
- Day 9 asks how fast the issuer acted, which needs the event time set against the case's transfers: the next check.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the two questions and their two answers.
2. Read the Tether statement, then the two rows of the table: what each read gives.
3. Read the sentence and point at its two parts: what the chain shows, what it does not.

**Sources**
- @tether_usdttroncontract_2026
- @tether_tethertokensource_2017
- @tether_freeze344m_2026

:::

## Check: the freeze came two hours late {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

Back to the case. `TCase…` received the victim's 2,500 USDT and swept it at 10:32. At 12:30 the same day, USDT's contract logs `AddedBlackList` for `TCase…`. Today, `isBlackListed(TCase…)` returns true.

**Write one line:** did the freeze stop the victim's money? What do you tell the agent?

::: {.fragment}
**Answer:** no. The freeze came about two hours after the sweep, so the 2,500 USDT had already left; the freeze holds only what was still at the address [@tether_tethertokensource_2017]. Tell the agent: frozen at today's block, empty when frozen; follow the sweep to the exchange, which holds the records for the deposit [@tether_usdttroncontract_2026].

**Part 2 in one line:** on Tron, the issuer is the gatekeeper for USDT, and every freeze answer carries its block and time.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide closes part 2 with a check every student answers: set the freeze time against the transfers. It matters here because "the address is frozen" sounds like "the money is safe", and the times show it is not. Emphasize that the status is true and the money is gone at the same time.

**Key Points**
- Expected answer: no. The sweep at 10:32 moved the whole balance; the freeze at 12:30 came after it. A freeze stops the address from sending, so it holds only what was still there.
- What to tell the agent: the address is blacklisted at today's block, but it was empty when frozen. The lead is the sweep's destination, the exchange, which holds the records for the deposit (04-FO).
- This is day 9's question: freezable, by which issuer, and how fast? Here the answer to "how fast" is: too late for this deposit.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the case with its three times.
2. Give every student thirty seconds to write one line.
3. Take a show of hands for yes and no, then reveal the answer and the part 2 line.

**Sources**
- @tether_tethertokensource_2017
- @tether_usdttroncontract_2026

:::

## Permissioned: the operator decides who writes {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

- **Trust moves again** [@androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018; @hyperledger_blockchainplatformenterprise_2023]: Bitcoin rests on costly work, Ethereum on stake; a **permissioned ledger** rests on **identity and policy**, and only the organizations the operator admits take part.
- **Everyone is known by certificate:** in Hyperledger Fabric, a **membership service provider (MSP)** maps each participant to a certificate from its organization's authority [@androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018].
- **A policy says whose signatures count:** an **endorsement policy** names which organizations' peers must sign a transaction before it is valid [@androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018].
- **An orderer puts it in a block:** the **ordering service** "orders it with other endorsed transactions, and packages them all into a block" [@hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_orderingservice_2026].
- **Final when enough agree:** known members can agree without mining [@ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016; @yaga_blockchaintechnologyoverview_2018]:
  - **Raft** [@ongaro_searchunderstandableconsensus_2014], Fabric's recommended orderer, is crash fault tolerant: it keeps going while a majority of ordering nodes stay up [@hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_orderingservice_2026].
  - **PBFT** [@castro_practicalbyzantinefault_1999] is Byzantine fault tolerant: it keeps going while under a third of the nodes lie; Fabric 3.0 added a BFT orderer of this kind [@hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_orderingservice_2026].
- For the analyst: the gatekeeper is the **operator**. It admits members, writes the policy, and it and its members keep the ledger.

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide turns from an open ledger with a gatekeeping issuer to a ledger that is closed by design, and defines the four parts the rest of the lesson uses. It matters here because bank, government and central-bank systems are built this way. Emphasize that trust rests on identity and policy, set by an operator.

**Key Points**
- Day 1 (01-CM) showed that trust moves rather than disappears: to work on Bitcoin, to stake on Ethereum. On a permissioned ledger it moves to identity and policy, because the operator admits every member.
- The MSP ties every participant to a certificate, so every member is named.
- The endorsement policy decides whose peers must sign for a transaction to be valid. The Fabric demo takes peers offline to show a write failing for want of them.
- The ordering service (the orderer) puts endorsed transactions into blocks; it is a role the operator runs.
- Day 1 said known members are final as soon as enough agree. Raft and PBFT are the two families behind that. Raft, Fabric's recommended orderer, survives nodes that crash, as long as a majority stays up; it assumes no node lies. PBFT survives nodes that lie, as long as fewer than a third do. Fabric added a BFT orderer in version 3.0.
- So the operator admits members and keeps the records.

**Walkthrough**
1. Ask: on Tron, who can join? (Anyone.) On a permissioned ledger? (Only whom the operator admits.)
2. Read the four bold terms in order: MSP, endorsement policy, orderer, then the two consensus families.
3. Ask: a Raft orderer has three nodes and one fails. Does the ledger stop? (Expected answer: no; two of three is a majority.)

**Sources**
- @androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018
- @hyperledger_blockchainplatformenterprise_2023
- @hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_orderingservice_2026
- @ongaro_searchunderstandableconsensus_2014
- @castro_practicalbyzantinefault_1999
- @ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016
- @yaga_blockchaintechnologyoverview_2018

:::

## The trace stops at the operator's edge {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%"}

- **An outsider sees nothing:** no public node, no explorer, no copy of the ledger.
- **A member sees its channels:** a **channel** is a ledger shared by some members; it keeps whole transactions "confidential within a set of organizations" [@hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_privatedata_2022].
- **Some members see less:** a **private data collection** lets "a defined subset of organizations on a channel" read the data. Every other peer on the channel gets only a hash of it [@hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_privatedata_2022].
- **The orderer** "does not see the private data" [@hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_privatedata_2022].
- For the analyst: an on-chain trace **stops at the operator's edge**. The records are real, but they sit with the operator and its members.

:::

::: {.column width="42%"}

```{dot}
digraph Edge {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=12];
  edge [color="#64748b", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];
  subgraph cluster_net {
    label="Operator's network"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=10; style="rounded,dashed"; color="#e53e3e";
    C [label="Channel members:\nfull transactions", fillcolor="#dcfce7"];
    PD [label="Collection members:\nprivate data", fillcolor="#dbeafe"];
    H [label="Other members:\nhash only", fillcolor="#fef3c7"];
  }
  X [label="Outside analyst:\nnothing", fillcolor="#e5e7eb"];
  X -> C [style=dashed, color="#e53e3e", label="no access"];
  C -> PD [style=invis];
  PD -> H [style=invis];
}
```

:::

::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide is the core of the second case: what an analyst can and cannot see on a permissioned ledger. It matters here because analysts will meet funds that enter a bank ledger, a CBDC or an enterprise network and vanish from public view. Emphasize the sentence "the trace stops at the operator's edge."

**Key Points**
- An outsider has no node and no explorer to read, because the operator gives copies only to members.
- A channel is a ledger only some members share, so each member sees its own channels.
- A private data collection narrows it further: the collection's members read the data, and the other peers on the channel hold only a hash of it.
- The orderer, defined on the last slide, orders transactions without seeing private data.
- The records exist and sit with the operator and its members; obtaining them is a matter for agents and prosecutors, outside this course.

**Walkthrough**
1. Walk the diagram from the outside in.
2. Ask: a member is on the channel but not in the collection. What does it hold? (A hash of the private data, not the data.)

**Sources**
- @hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_privatedata_2022

:::

## What each reader can see {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

| Ledger | Who can read it | Who is named | Who can stop a payment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bitcoin | Anyone | No one; addresses only | No one on chain |
| Ethereum or Tron, USDT | Anyone | No one; addresses only | The issuer, by freezing [@tether_tethertokensource_2017; @tether_usdttroncontract_2026] |
| Permissioned, as a member | Your channels; hashes of others' private data | Every member, by certificate | The operator and the policy [@androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018] |
| Permissioned, as an outsider | Nothing | Unknown to you | The operator |

:::

For the analyst: on an open ledger you can trace to the edge of an exchange or an issuer. On a closed one, the edge is the network itself.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide sets every ledger met so far side by side by what an analyst can see. It matters here because students need one picture to say, for any case, where their view ends. Emphasize the last row: from outside, a permissioned ledger is blank.

**Key Points**
- Open ledgers: everyone reads, no one is named, and only a token issuer can stop a token.
- Permissioned ledgers: members read what the channel and the collections allow, everyone is named by certificate, and the operator controls through the policy.
- The outsider row is the analyst's usual seat.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read across each row.
2. Ask: which row is a bank's internal ledger, seen by you? (Permissioned, as an outsider.)

**Sources**
- @tether_tethertokensource_2017
- @tether_usdttroncontract_2026
- @androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018

:::

## Check: funds leave Tron for a bank's ledger {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

A second case. A T-address sends 40,000 USDT to an address that a bank publishes as its way in to a tokenized-deposit ledger the bank runs on Fabric. No more transfers appear on Tron.

**Write one line:** what can you still say, and where does your view end?

::: {.fragment}
**Answer:** everything up to the edge: the transfer, its block and time, and that it went to the bank's published address. You can name the bank as the operator, and that its ledger holds the next records; you cannot read them, because an outsider sees nothing [@hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_privatedata_2022; @androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018].

**Part 3 in one line:** on a permissioned ledger, the operator is the gatekeeper, and the trace stops at its edge.
:::

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide closes part 3 with a check every student answers: a trace that leaves an open ledger for a closed one. It matters here because "the trail goes cold" is the wrong report; the right one names the operator who holds the next records. Emphasize what the analyst can still say.

**Key Points**
- Expected answer: the analyst can state the Tron transfer and its block, that it went to the bank's published address, and that the bank operates the ledger that holds the next records. The analyst cannot read that ledger from outside.
- The case is made up; tokenized deposits on a permissioned ledger are one way banks use the technology, and the reading holds for any operator.
- Naming the operator is a complete answer: obtaining the records is for agents and prosecutors, outside this course.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the case.
2. Give every student thirty seconds to write one line.
3. Take two answers, ask whether either said "the trail goes cold", then reveal the answer and the part 3 line.

**Sources**
- @hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_privatedata_2022
- @androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018

:::

## A CBDC is a ledger a central bank runs {.smaller}

- A **central bank digital currency (CBDC)** is money a central bank issues in digital form [@atlanticcouncil_cbdctracker_2026]. Run on a ledger, it is a permissioned ledger with the central bank as operator.
- **Status:** most countries are exploring one; three have launched one (the Bahamas, Jamaica, Nigeria), and the US is the only G20 country not exploring one [@atlanticcouncil_cbdctracker_2026] [May 2026]{.asof}.
- **mBridge, a shared CBDC ledger:** a platform "based on a new blockchain – the mBridge Ledger," compatible with the Ethereum Virtual Machine. Each founding central bank ran a validating node; the BIS handed the project to its partners in October 2024 [@l34_bis_mbridge_mvp_2024].
- For the analyst: the central bank is the gatekeeper, and the trace stops at its edge.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide places CBDCs in the lesson's frame: a CBDC on a ledger is a permissioned ledger with a central bank as operator. It matters here because foreign CBDCs, and cross-border platforms like mBridge, are where a US analyst may see funds leave public view. Emphasize that the analyst can name the operator but cannot read the ledger.

**Key Points**
- A CBDC is central-bank money in digital form; when it runs on a ledger, everything part 3 said about operators applies, with the central bank as operator.
- Most countries are exploring one, three have launched, and the US is the only G20 country not exploring one, per the Atlantic Council's tracker as last updated in May 2026. The tracker's full counts (exploring, pilots) change often; read the tracker for the current figures.
- mBridge is a shared ledger whose validating nodes were run by central banks; the BIS left it in October 2024.

**Walkthrough**
1. Ask: a foreign central bank runs its CBDC on a ledger. Can you trace payments on it as you trace USDT on Tron? (Expected answer: no. The central bank is the operator and decides who can read it. You can name the operator, but the trace stops at its edge.)

**Sources**
- @atlanticcouncil_cbdctracker_2026
- @l34_bis_mbridge_mvp_2024

:::

## Fabric demo: watch the gatekeeper work {.smaller}

The instructor runs a live Hyperledger Fabric network, a permissioned platform [@hyperledger_blockchainplatformenterprise_2023]. In the demo, member organizations share a channel to issue and check diplomas. Watch for three things:

1. **Who signed it?** Each transaction names the organization that endorsed it, by its MSP identity [@androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018].
2. **Who decides?** The endorsement policy names whose peers must sign a write; without enough of them, the write is not valid [@androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018]. The demo takes peers offline to show it.
3. **Who can see it?** You see it because the instructor admitted you. Without a certificate, there is nothing to read.

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide sets up the instructor's Fabric demo that closes the day. It matters here because students see a permissioned ledger working: identity, policy and access, controlled by an operator. Emphasize the three questions; the demo answers each one live.

**Key Points**
- Every transaction names its endorsing organization by MSP identity.
- An endorsement policy decides which organizations must sign; with too few peers up, writes fail.
- Membership and endorsement are separate: the policy decides whose endorsement counts, so a member may read and propose without being one the policy needs.
- Access itself is the gatekeeper: no certificate, no view.

**Walkthrough**
1. Hand the three questions to students to answer during the demo.
2. After the demo, ask each question aloud and take answers.

**Sources**
- @hyperledger_blockchainplatformenterprise_2023
- @androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018

:::

## Practice: name the gatekeeper for three records {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .85em;"}

For each record, name the gatekeeper, say what it can do (stop the payment, see the records, or both), and say what you can still read from outside.

1. **Tron.** A T-address holds 12,000 USDT. It received the USDT yesterday and has sent nothing since.
2. **Bitcoin.** A `bc1…` address received 0.5 BTC an hour ago, in a block with three confirmations.
3. **A central bank's ledger.** A payment in a country's CBDC, run on a permissioned ledger the central bank operates.

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
The four parts are done; this slide has students apply the lesson's one question to three records. It matters here because the analyst's first move on any ledger is to name who can stop or see a payment. Emphasize that "no one" is a valid gatekeeper answer.

**Key Points**
- Each record is a second case of something the lesson worked: record 1 of USDT on Tron (part 2), record 2 of the open ledgers in the comparison table, record 3 of the CBDC slide (part 4).
- The answers, with their reasons, are on the next slide; keep it hidden until students have written theirs.

**Walkthrough**
1. Give students three minutes in pairs to write one line per record.
2. Take an answer for record 1 first, then move on.

**Sources**
- @tether_usdttroncontract_2026
- @atlanticcouncil_cbdctracker_2026

:::

## Answers: three gatekeepers, what each can see {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size: .8em;"}

| Record | Gatekeeper | Can it stop the payment? | What you can read from outside |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Tron USDT** | Tether, through USDT's owner wallet [@tether_usdttroncontract_2026] | Yes: the balance is still there, so a freeze would hold it | Everything: the transfers, the balance, and any freeze, each with its block |
| **2. Bitcoin** | No one on chain | No: no issuer, no operator; the next gatekeeper is an exchange the coins reach (04-FO) | Everything on chain; no one is named |
| **3. CBDC** | The central bank, as operator [@atlanticcouncil_cbdctracker_2026] | Yes, by its policy | Nothing: the trace stops at its edge; name the operator |

: {tbl-colwidths="[14,24,30,32]"}

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide gives the practice's answers, each with its gatekeeper, what it can do, and the analyst's view. It matters here because the reasons, not just the names, are what students carry into the lab and day 9. Emphasize record 1's reason: a freeze holds only what is still there.

**Key Points**
- Record 1: Tether is the gatekeeper, because USDT's owner can blacklist the address; since the 12,000 USDT has not moved, a freeze would hold it. The analyst reads everything, and dates every freeze answer.
- Record 2: on Bitcoin no one on chain can stop a payment; the first gatekeeper is the exchange the coins reach, as 04-FO showed.
- Record 3: the central bank operates the ledger, so it can stop a payment through its policy and it alone decides who reads. From outside, the analyst names the operator and stops there.

**Walkthrough**
1. Reveal the slide after students have written their three lines.
2. Read each row, and ask a pair who wrote something different to say why.

**Sources**
- @tether_usdttroncontract_2026
- @atlanticcouncil_cbdctracker_2026

:::

## Review: every record has a gatekeeper {.smaller}

[]{#what-to-carry-out-of-this-lesson}

::: {style="font-size: .8em;"}

**The objective:** for any ledger in a case, name the gatekeeper, say what it can do, and say what you can still read from outside. Answer each question from memory before the answer appears.

**1. A T-address and a 0x address carry the same 20 bytes. What does that suggest?**

::: {.fragment}
One key made both, so probably one controller: a lead to confirm [@tron_accounts_2026].
:::

**2. An address with no TRX moves USDT. Who paid?**

::: {.fragment}
Another account, by delegating Energy or by sending TRX to burn; that payer is a link [@tron_resourcemodel_2026].
:::

**3. The case's T-address is frozen today. Is the victim's money safe?**

::: {.fragment}
Not necessarily: a freeze holds only what was there when it came. Set its block and time against the transfers [@tether_usdttroncontract_2026].
:::

**4. Funds enter a permissioned ledger. Where does your view end?**

::: {.fragment}
At the operator's edge. Name the operator; its records hold the rest [@hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_privatedata_2022].
:::

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide reviews the lesson against its objective: four questions, one per part's main idea, answered from memory before each answer appears. It matters here because recalling an answer fixes it better than hearing a summary, and the questions show whether students can now do what the opening promised. Emphasize question 3: the wrong belief the case was built to correct.

**Key Points**
- Question 1 is part 1's check: one key behind two address forms.
- Question 2 is the Energy slide's wrong idea, asked again: the sender is not always the payer.
- Question 3 is part 2's check: a true status and an empty address at once.
- Question 4 is part 3's line: the operator's edge.
- No new facts appear here; every answer was taught on an earlier slide.

**Walkthrough**
1. Read the objective.
2. For each question, give students a few seconds to answer aloud or on paper, then reveal the answer.
3. Ask the class the objective as a question: given a ledger, can you name its gatekeeper and your view?

**Sources**
- @tron_accounts_2026
- @tron_resourcemodel_2026
- @tether_usdttroncontract_2026
- @hyperledgerfabricdevelopers_privatedata_2022

:::

## Next: a transfer, a sweep, a freeze {.smaller}

[]{#this-afternoon-a-transfer-a-sweep-a-freeze}

::: {style="font-size: .88em;"}

This afternoon's lab gives you a snapshot of Tron data, read from java-tron, Tron's open-source node [@tronprotocol_javatron_2026]. You do the three reads part 2 worked, on real data:

| Where | What you do with today's reading |
| --- | --- |
| **Day 5 lab** | Read a USDT transfer, a deposit and its sweep (and who paid), and an issuer freeze, dated to the snapshot's block |
| **Fabric demo** | Watch the operator admit, endorse and hide, live |
| Day 9 | A Tron stablecoin trace: "Freezable? Which issuer, and how fast?" |
| Day 10 | The final trace, with Tron USDT |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

**Bottom line:** every ledger has a gatekeeper. Name it, say what it can stop and see, and say where your own view ends.

:::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
The review checked the objective; this slide gives the lesson's bottom line and names what comes next without teaching it. It matters here because the afternoon lab applies part 2 to real data, and the Fabric demo shows part 3 live. Emphasize that every lab answer about a freeze carries the snapshot's block.

**Key Points**
- The snapshot comes from java-tron, the open-source node. Its three reads are the three part 2 worked: a transfer, a deposit and its sweep with its payer, a freeze.
- A freeze answer from the lab carries the snapshot's block and date, because a freeze can be lifted later.
- The Fabric demo closes the day.
- Day 9 returns to "Freezable? Which issuer, and how fast?"; day 10's final trace includes Tron USDT.

**Walkthrough**

2. Ask: why does a freeze answer from the lab carry the snapshot's block and date? (Expected answer: a freeze can be lifted later, so the status is true only at the block read.)
3. Close on the bottom line.

**Sources**
- @tronprotocol_javatron_2026

## Scenario



:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
- A number of different groups all need access to records of cargo handoffs.
- They must coordinate on:
  - Who transferred custody.
  - When the handoff occurred.
  - Which documents were approved.
- They cooperate, but they are not all on the same team:
  - Some are competitors.
  - Some are regulators.
  - Some should see only part of the data.
- Do the systems we've been discussing work here?
  - What are key aspects of an ideal system in this scenario?
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This opening scenario establishes the kind of cross-organization record-sharing problem permissioned ledgers are meant to solve. It matters here because the rest of the lesson explains which design features let many known parties share one authoritative record without handing control to a single company. Emphasize that the challenge is not just storing data, but assigning rights, visibility, and authority across different roles.

**Key Points**
- Multiple organizations need one shared handoff record while retaining different permissions.
- Some parties should write, some should only read, and some should audit.
- The core design question is who gets to do what and who decides those roles.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@yaga_blockchaintechnologyoverview_2018; @ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Agenda

1. Why permissioned ledgers/systems
2. What changes when participation is centrally controlled
3. Identity, membership, and policy as core mechanisms
4. Consensus and finality under known membership
5. Governance
6. Operational risk
7. Problem fit




::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This agenda slide gives students the lesson roadmap so they can see how technical mechanisms and governance questions fit together. It matters here because permissioned systems are easiest to understand when identity, policy, consensus, and operations are treated as one stack. Emphasize that the lesson moves from problem fit through mechanism design to operational risk.

**Key Points**
- The lesson progresses from motivation to mechanism to governance and risk.
- Identity, membership, and policy will be treated as first-class system components.
- Problem fit matters because a permissioned ledger is not automatically the right answer.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@bano_consensusageblockchains_2017; @yaga_blockchaintechnologyoverview_2018

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Why Not A Shared Database?

- If one company runs the database, everyone else must trust that company not to:
  - Edit or hide history.
  - Expose competitor data.
  - Lock others out during a dispute.
- If everyone gets broad administrative access, the system becomes hard to govern and easy to misuse.
- Simple replication helps availability, but it does not solve authority, visibility, or finality.
- An append-only shared ledger also helps with audit:
  - History is preserved across organizations instead of overwritten.
  - Sensitive data can remain off-chain while hashes or commitments support later verification.

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Key idea:** permissioned ledgers fit when multiple known organizations need a shared record without a single administrative owner.
:::


::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide explains why a simple shared database does not fully solve a multi-organization trust problem. It matters here because students need to see that replication and administration are not the same as neutral shared control. Emphasize that authority, visibility, and dispute handling remain unsolved if one party still owns the database.

**Key Points**
- A single-operator database forces everyone else to trust that operator's control plane.
- Broad admin access for all parties creates governance and misuse problems instead of solving them.
- Append-only shared records help with auditability across organizational boundaries.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016; @androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## What Changes

- The hard problem shifts from "how do we let anyone join safely?" to "how do we control participation and authority safely?"

| Dimension | Permissionless | Permissioned |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Participation | Open | Curated |
| Identity | Pseudonymous / economic | Named / authenticated |
| Sybil resistance | Resource cost | Admission control |
| Ordering | Chosen by miner / proposer selection | Often handled by explicit leaders or ordering services |
| Finality | Often probabilistic | Often deterministic |
| Governance | Social + economic | Administrative + policy-driven |
| Failure Concentration | Broadly distributed influence | More risk from small control-plane failures |


::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide shows how the core problem changes once membership is known and curated. It matters here because permissioned design replaces open-admission defenses with identity, policy, and administrative controls. Emphasize that the trust model changes, not the need for careful system design.

**Key Points**
- Permissioned systems trade open participation for curated admission and explicit authority.
- Sybil resistance shifts from economic cost to admission control and identity verification.
- Finality and governance often become more deterministic because participants are known in advance.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@yaga_blockchaintechnologyoverview_2018; @ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Key Components {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="68%"}
  - **Identity And Membership:** The mechanisms that decide who a participant is and what standing they have in the network.
    - A permissioned system only works if every action can be tied back to a recognized participant with the right role.
  - **Policy And Governance:** The rules that decide who may act, what approvals are required, and who can change the network itself.
    - Good consensus does not help if weak rules let the wrong people approve transactions.
  - **Core Operation:** The day-to-day transaction path that moves requests from proposal to shared committed history.
    - Turns approved requests into one shared history that authorized participants can rely on.
:::
::: {.column width="32%"}
```{=html}

      <div style="padding:0.28rem 0.38rem;border-radius:10px;background:#fde68a;border:1px solid #f59e0b;font-size:0.74em;text-align:center;">Approve</div>
```

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide groups the three pillars of a permissioned ledger into one picture before the class studies them in detail. It matters here because students should understand that identity, policy, and transaction processing are inseparable in this setting. Emphasize that strong consensus is not enough if identity or governance is weak.

**Key Points**
- Identity and membership determine who the system recognizes and trusts to act.
- Policy and governance define what those recognized parties may do.
- Core operation turns approved requests into one shared committed history.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@bano_consensusageblockchains_2017; @androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Open vs Curated Admission

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
- Open systems ask:
  - How do we stop one actor from creating many identities?
- Permissioned systems ask:
  - Who is allowed in, and who decides?
- Permissioned admission adds overhead up front:
  - In return, it enables stronger accountability, traceability, and role-based trust later.
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{=html}
<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;align-items:flex-start;gap:1rem;max-width:520px;margin:0 auto;">
  <div style="flex:1;max-width:200px;border:2px solid #93c5fd;border-radius:16px;background:#eff6ff;padding:0.7rem 0.75rem;">
    <div style="font-weight:700;font-size:0.9em;text-align:center;color:#1d4ed8;margin-bottom:0.45rem;">Permissionless Join Path</div>
    <div style="display:flex;flex-direction:column;align-items:center;gap:0.28rem;">
      <div style="width:100%;padding:0.38rem 0.45rem;border-radius:10px;background:#dbeafe;border:1px solid #93c5fd;font-size:0.75em;text-align:center;">Generate Keypair</div>
      <div style="font-size:1.05em;line-height:1;color:#64748b;">↓</div>
      <div style="width:100%;padding:0.38rem 0.45rem;border-radius:10px;background:#bfdbfe;border:1px solid #60a5fa;font-size:0.75em;text-align:center;">Connect To Network</div>
      <div style="font-size:1.05em;line-height:1;color:#64748b;">↓</div>
      <div style="width:100%;padding:0.38rem 0.45rem;border-radius:10px;background:#93c5fd;border:1px solid #3b82f6;font-size:0.75em;text-align:center;">Participate Under Public Rules</div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div style="flex:1;max-width:220px;border:2px solid #86efac;border-radius:16px;background:#f0fdf4;padding:0.7rem 0.75rem;">
    <div style="font-weight:700;font-size:0.9em;text-align:center;color:#15803d;margin-bottom:0.45rem;">Permissioned Join Path</div>
    <div style="display:flex;flex-direction:column;align-items:center;gap:0.28rem;">
      <div style="width:100%;padding:0.38rem 0.45rem;border-radius:10px;background:#dcfce7;border:1px solid #86efac;font-size:0.75em;text-align:center;">Identify Applicant</div>
      <div style="font-size:1.05em;line-height:1;color:#64748b;">↓</div>
      <div style="width:100%;padding:0.38rem 0.45rem;border-radius:10px;background:#bbf7d0;border:1px solid #4ade80;font-size:0.75em;text-align:center;">Vet And Approve</div>
      <div style="font-size:1.05em;line-height:1;color:#64748b;">↓</div>
      <div style="width:100%;padding:0.38rem 0.45rem;border-radius:10px;background:#86efac;border:1px solid #22c55e;font-size:0.75em;text-align:center;">Issue Credential</div>
      <div style="font-size:1.05em;line-height:1;color:#64748b;">↓</div>
      <div style="width:100%;padding:0.38rem 0.45rem;border-radius:10px;background:#4ade80;border:1px solid #16a34a;font-size:0.75em;text-align:center;">Assign Role</div>
      <div style="font-size:1.05em;line-height:1;color:#64748b;">↓</div>
      <div style="width:100%;padding:0.38rem 0.45rem;border-radius:10px;background:#22c55e;border:1px solid #15803d;font-size:0.75em;text-align:center;color:#052e16;">Connect To Network</div>
      <div style="font-size:1.05em;line-height:1;color:#64748b;">↓</div>
      <div style="width:100%;padding:0.38rem 0.45rem;border-radius:10px;background:#22c55e;border:1px solid #15803d;font-size:0.75em;text-align:center;color:#052e16;">Participate Under Tracked Identity</div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>
```
:::
::::


::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide contrasts open admission with curated admission so students can see what overhead permissioned systems deliberately accept. It matters here because stronger accountability later depends on heavier vetting earlier. Emphasize that front-loaded admission work is the price of role-based trust and traceability.

**Key Points**
- Open systems worry about fake identity multiplication, while permissioned systems worry about who gets admitted at all.
- Curated admission adds vetting, credential issuance, and role assignment before participation begins.
- The payoff is stronger accountability and traceability once the network is running.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018; @ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Trust Shifts

- In PoW, security relies on **costly work**: 
  - Hardware investment and electricity expenditure impose real-world cost to influence block production.
- In PoS, security relies on **stake and penalties**: 
  - Locked capital and slashing expose participants to direct financial loss for misbehavior.
- In permissioned systems, security relies on **identity, policy, and governance**: 
  - Vetted participants, assigned roles, and revocable access replace open-admission economics.
- Intuition: in an ongoing consortium, bad behavior damages future cooperation, contracts, reputation, and access in ways that pseudonymous open networks cannot rely on.

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
**Key idea:** a permissioned ledger still distributes trust, but it distributes it through institutions and policy instead of open economic competition.
:::


::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide explains how the basis of trust shifts from open economic competition to institutional identity and governance. It matters here because students have already seen PoW and PoS, and now need a third trust model for comparison. Emphasize that permissioned systems still distribute trust, but through known organizations and enforceable policies.

**Key Points**
- PoW relies on costly work, and PoS relies on stake plus penalties.
- Permissioned systems rely on vetted identity, assigned roles, and revocable access.
- Institutional relationships and future cooperation become part of the security story.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018; @hyperledger_blockchainplatformenterprise_2023

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Identity

- Identity is not just convenience; it defines who the system recognizes and what their actions mean.
- In this setting:
  - An **Organization** is a consortium member such as a carrier, port, regulator, or insurer
  - A **User / Operator** is a person or service acting on behalf of that organization
  - A **Node** is a software instance run by an organization to submit, approve, order, or store ledger activity
  - A **Credential** is the cryptographic proof tying those actions to an organization and role
- Messages, approvals, and administrative actions are meaningful only if identities are verifiable.
- If identity is weak, all later policy checks become weak too.
- Example: a "Port Operator reviewer" and a "Port Operator admin" should not be treated as the same authority.


::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide defines identity precisely enough for policy enforcement to make sense. It matters here because all later approval, ordering, and governance actions depend on knowing who is acting in what capacity. Emphasize that organizations, users, nodes, and credentials are related but not interchangeable.

**Key Points**
- Organizations, operators, nodes, and credentials play different roles in the system.
- Credentials bind actions to recognized entities and assigned roles.
- Weak identity undermines every later policy check built on top of it.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018; @ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Membership Lifecycle

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
- Permissioned membership is not a one-time setup. Implementations must decide
  - **How new members are verified:** usually some combination of identity proofing, organizational approval, and role assignment before any credential is issued.
  - **How often credentials expire:** often measured in months, not decades; short-lived operational certificates and longer-lived organizational roots are both common.
  - **How quickly revocation propagates:** ideally minutes to hours; stale admin access is a major threat in a permissioned network.
  - **How audits and periodic reviews are conducted:** many organizations review access quarterly or at least annually, and high-risk roles are often checked more often.



:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
```{dot}
digraph MembershipLifecycle {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", color="#94a3b8", fontsize=10];
  edge [color="#64748b", penwidth=1.3];

  A [label="Join Request", fillcolor="#dbeafe"];
  B [label="Verify", fillcolor="#bfdbfe"];
  C [label="Issue", fillcolor="#93c5fd"];
  D [label="Use", fillcolor="#bbf7d0"];
  E [label="Review", fillcolor="#fde68a"];
  F [label="Renew / Rotate", fillcolor="#fcd34d"];
  G [label="Revoke", fillcolor="#fecaca"];

  A -> B -> C -> D -> E -> F;
  F -> D;
  E -> G [color="#dc2626"];
}
```
:::
::::


::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide shows that membership management is a continuous control process rather than a one-time onboarding event. It matters here because expired credentials, stale admin rights, and slow revocation can all create system-wide failures. Emphasize that join, review, renew, and revoke are all part of security.

**Key Points**
- Membership must cover verification, issuance, review, renewal, and revocation.
- Credential lifetime and revocation speed directly affect risk.
- Operational reviews are necessary because identities and roles change over time.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@castro_practicalbyzantinefault_1999; @ongaro_searchunderstandableconsensus_2014

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Roles and Duties {.smaller}

| Role | Responsibility | Why Separate? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Client / app | Submit business requests | Business activity ≠ admin control |
| Validator / endorser | Approve transactions | Requesters can't self-approve |
| Orderer / sequencer | Establish order | Sequencing ≠ business logic |
| Administrator | Manage config & membership | Power isn't concentrated in one team |
| Auditor / observer | Review history & compliance | Oversight stays independent |


::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide separates system roles so students can see how permissioned safety often depends on not concentrating authority. It matters here because blending business activity, approval, sequencing, and administration can turn one compromise into total control. Emphasize the security value of role separation.

**Key Points**
- Submitting requests, approving them, ordering them, and governing the network are distinct jobs.
- Separation of duties limits the blast radius of a compromised identity or team.
- Independent audit roles help keep oversight separate from direct operational power.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018; @ongaro_searchunderstandableconsensus_2014

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Consensus

- Because participants are known, permissioned systems can use classical CFT or BFT techniques.
- That usually means:
  - Leaders or coordinators.
  - Quorums.
  - Signed approvals.
  - Deterministic commit rules.
- The system counts **approved signatures from known members**.
  - It no longer needs mining or staking at all; access control and transaction policies replace them.
- Usually not everyone votes:
  - Read-only or audit-only participants typically do not.
  - A designated subset of approving members usually does.
  - Governance committees may be the same as, or different from, transaction approvers.



::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide introduces permissioned consensus as a known-membership coordination problem rather than an open-entry contest. It matters here because students should connect classical CFT/BFT techniques to the governance setting they now understand. Emphasize that signed approvals from named participants replace mining or staking.

**Key Points**
- Permissioned systems often use classical leader, quorum, and signed-approval techniques.
- Not every participant needs to vote; roles determine who actually approves transactions.
- Access control and policy replace open-admission Sybil defenses such as PoW or PoS.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016; @androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Deterministic Finality

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
- **Deterministic finality:** because CFT/BFT algorithms work with known participants, once the required signatures are collected and the quorum rule is met, the transaction is final: no waiting, no probability, no risk of reordering.
- **Contrast with PoW:** PoW finality is probabilistic. Confidence grows as computing investment accumulates on top of a block. Permissioned systems avoid mining, forking, and longest-chain races entirely.
  - You *could* build a permissioned PoW ledger, but it creates extra overhead for no benefit.
- **Contrast with PoS:** permissioned approaches have more overlap with PoS, but PoS must handle unknown validators. It relies on staking, randomness, and economic penalties to make misbehavior costly. Permissioned systems replace these with identity and policy.
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
```{dot}
digraph DeterministicFinality {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];
  edge [color="#64748b"];

  P [label="Proposal", fillcolor="#dbeafe"];
  A [label="Required Signed Approvals", fillcolor="#dcfce7"];
  Q [label="Quorum Rule Met", fillcolor="#fef3c7"];
  C [label="Commit Is Final", fillcolor="#fee2e2"];

  P -> A -> Q -> C;
}
```
:::
::::


::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide explains why permissioned systems can often offer deterministic finality. It matters here because finality behavior is one of the biggest practical differences from public-chain designs students have already seen. Emphasize that once the required approvals and quorum rules are satisfied, there is no waiting for probabilistic confidence to grow.

**Key Points**
- Deterministic finality means a committed transaction is final as soon as the protocol's threshold is met.
- Permissioned systems avoid mining races and longest-chain competition.
- Identity and policy replace the economic machinery public systems use to discipline participants.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016; @yaga_blockchaintechnologyoverview_2018

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Transaction Path

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Identity check:** Does the requester have a valid role and credential?
- **Proposal / submission:** A participant submits a business event, such as a cargo handoff.
- **Required approvals:** Policy determines which organizations or nodes must approve; sometimes one organization, sometimes several.
- **Ordering / sequencing:** An ordering service or leader-based cluster places accepted requests into a consistent order.
- **Validation against policy:** Committing or validating nodes check that the ordered request still satisfies policy and state rules.
- **Commit:** The record is written to the shared ledger.

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{dot}
digraph GenericPath {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10];
  edge [color="#64748b"];

  C1 [label="Submitting Org", fillcolor="#dbeafe"];
  I [label="Identity Check", fillcolor="#bfdbfe"];
  A1 [label="Approving Org A", fillcolor="#dcfce7"];
  A2 [label="Approving Org B", fillcolor="#bbf7d0"];
  O [label="Ordering Service\n(Single Node or Small Cluster)", fillcolor="#fef3c7"];
  V [label="Validating / Committing Nodes", fillcolor="#fde68a"];
  L [label="Shared Ledger", fillcolor="#fee2e2"];

  C1 -> I;
  I -> A1;
  I -> A2;
  {A1 A2} -> O;
  O -> V -> L;
}
```
:::
::::



::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide turns the permissioned model into an operational transaction pipeline. It matters here because students should be able to trace how a business request becomes a committed shared record. Emphasize that identity checks, approvals, ordering, validation, and commit are separate steps with different control points.

**Key Points**
- Requests are checked for identity and role before entering the approval path.
- Policy determines which organizations or nodes must approve a given action.
- Ordering and validation convert approved requests into one consistent committed history.

**Walkthrough**
1. Identity check: verify the requester has the right credential and role.
2. Proposal and approval: submit the event and collect the required organizational signoffs.
3. Order and validate: place approved requests into a consistent sequence and confirm they still satisfy policy.
4. Commit: write the accepted result to the shared ledger.

**Sources**
@ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016; @yaga_blockchaintechnologyoverview_2018

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Policy Layers

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="54%"}
- In **permissionless systems**, security often rests on economics.
- In permissioned systems, much of the security story lives in **policy**:
  - Which organization may submit a shipment handoff.
  - Which organizations must approve that handoff.
  - Who may change consortium configuration.
  - Who may add or remove members.
- These are not side documents; they are part of the system's effective trust model.
- A participant may be allowed to read without writing, submit without approving, or approve without controlling policy.
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{dot}
digraph PolicyPyramid {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, margin="0.08,0.05"];
  edge [style=invis];

  G [label="May Change\nMembers / Policy", fillcolor="#fef3c7", width=1.45, height=0.5];
  A [label="May Approve\nTransactions", fillcolor="#86efac", width=1.9, height=0.5];
  S [label="May Submit\nTransactions", fillcolor="#bfdbfe", width=2.35, height=0.5];
  R [label="May Read /\nAudit", fillcolor="#dbeafe", width=2.8, height=0.5];

  G -> A -> S -> R;
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide explains that much of permissioned security lives in explicit policy, not only in the ordering protocol. It matters here because students may otherwise treat governance documents as external paperwork instead of part of the trust model. Emphasize that read, submit, approve, and administer are distinct powers that policy must define carefully.

**Key Points**
- Permissioned security depends on who may read, submit, approve, and govern.
- Policy is part of the effective trust model, not an afterthought.
- Different powers can and should be distributed across different groups.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@pishdar_denialofserviceattackspermissioned_2025; @androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Governance Boundary

- Governance decides who can change the people, rules, and thresholds.
- That makes governance part of the attack surface.
- In a permissioned system, "consensus" usually means some known set of members approves transactions and some service orders them under policy.
- Even if that transaction-approval and ordering path is sound, the system can still fail if governance is weak.
- Strong transaction consensus cannot compensate for:
  - Weak admission decisions.
  - Poor key management.
  - Ambiguous authority.
  - Unsafe upgrade procedures.
- Typical failure pattern: the ledger software works as designed, but the wrong people are allowed to change the rules.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Blockchain does not protect a permissioned network from bad governance.
:::


::: {.notes}

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide makes governance itself visible as a security boundary. It matters here because a technically correct transaction path can still be undone by weak membership control or unsafe rule changes. Emphasize that governance failures are not outside the system; they are one of its main attack surfaces.

**Key Points**
- Governance decides who can change members, thresholds, and operational rules.
- Weak admission, key management, or upgrade control can break the system even if consensus works as intended.
- Permissioned blockchains do not automatically protect against bad institutional decision-making.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@pishdar_denialofserviceattackspermissioned_2025; @androulaki_hyperledgerfabricdistributed_2018

:::

::::

:::: {.content-hidden}

## Governance Actions

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}

- Governance is a critical component of any blockchain, and it has substantial ramifications for the differences between permissioned and permissionless networks.

  - *Permissionless networks* upgrades depend on adoption decisions by each node.
    - Disagreements can result in hard forks, splitting into two separate blockchains or ledgers.
  - *Permissioned networks:* authorized governance members decide according to policy first, and then all managed members implement their instructions.
    - Forks are avoided, governance processes coordinate a single outcome across nodes.
    
:::
::: {.column width="35%"}
```{=html}
<div style="display:flex;flex-direction:column;gap:0.9rem;max-width:520px;margin:0 auto;">
  <div style="border:2px solid #93c5fd;border-radius:16px;background:#eff6ff;padding:0.7rem 0.8rem;">
    <div style="font-weight:700;font-size:0.9em;color:#1d4ed8;text-align:center;margin-bottom:0.45rem;">Permissionless Upgrade</div>
    <div style="display:flex;flex-direction:column;align-items:center;gap:0.28rem;margin-bottom:0.35rem;">
      <div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;gap:0.38rem;flex-wrap:wrap;max-width:270px;">
        <div style="width:17px;height:17px;border-radius:999px;background:#22c55e;border:2px solid #15803d;"></div>
        <div style="width:17px;height:17px;border-radius:999px;background:#22c55e;border:2px solid #15803d;"></div>
        <div style="width:17px;height:17px;border-radius:999px;background:#22c55e;border:2px solid #15803d;"></div>
        <div style="width:17px;height:17px;border-radius:999px;background:#22c55e;border:2px solid #15803d;"></div>
        <div style="width:17px;height:17px;border-radius:999px;background:#22c55e;border:2px solid #15803d;"></div>
        <div style="width:17px;height:17px;border-radius:999px;background:#22c55e;border:2px solid #15803d;"></div>
```

**Overall Slide Concept**
This slide compares how governance actions propagate in permissionless and permissioned environments. It matters here because upgrade and dispute resolution reveal how authority is actually exercised in each model. Emphasize that permissioned systems aim for one administratively chosen outcome, while permissionless systems may split when adoption diverges.

**Key Points**
- Permissionless upgrades depend on independent adoption decisions and can result in forks.
- Permissioned upgrades are typically decided administratively and then applied across managed members.
- Governance processes shape not just policy but how change enters the network at all.

**Walkthrough**
None

**Sources**
@yaga_blockchaintechnologyoverview_2018; @ukgovernmentchiefscientificadviser_distributedledgertechnology_2016

:::
